newsitem.title: GERMANY: German "shoeshiners on welfare" scheme slammed.
newsitem.headline: German "shoeshiners on welfare" scheme slammed.

text.p: A proposal by Germany's main employers' federation designed to encourage Germans to take the sort of low-pay jobs they have long shunned was roundly attacked on Thursday.

The scheme, put forward this week by the BDA employers' federation, would allow workers taking low-paid jobs to retain more of their welfare benefits than at present, thus removing a major barrier to more people accepting such work.

The BDA hopes such a move would create new takers for work such as waitressing, cleaning, gardening or -- that potent symbol of United States free enterprise, the shoe-shiner -- that at the moment are often done by moonlighters or not at all.

Trade unions and left-leaning politicians however dismissed the plan as an attempt by employers to secure cheap labour and as a disguised attack on the social state, which currently offers Germans a relatively high degree of welfare provision.
"The BDA's proposals to subsidise work in this way would pile pressure mercilessly on the wider jobs market," Dieter Hundt, president of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB), said in a statement.

Opposition Social Democrats (SDP) said an accompanying proposal by the BDA that unemployment benefit be limited to 12 months, with the jobless drawing only social benefit thereafter, was simply "new dressing for more welfare cuts".
"These are ideas that would only accentuate the current divisions in our society," said Ottmar Schreiner, deputy chairman of the parliamentary SPD.

BDA president Dieter Hundt said on Wednesday the scheme would mean a household with two children drawing 2,800 marks ($1,610) welfare would lose only 925 marks of their benefits instead of the current 1,285 marks if one parent had a net income of 1,500 marks.

Hundt said he hoped to be able to work with government ministries on the proposals and that the plan, which he believes could significantly reduce Germany's record jobless levels, could be implemented in the current year.

A spokesman for the Employment and Social Affairs Ministry in Bonn said however that while the government was prepared to discuss such ideas, it had not looked at the proposal in detail and was sceptical about allowing more outside income to be taken out of welfare benefit calculations.
"There clearly has to be a limit," the spokesman said.
